detail.abstract: In recent decades, the international development community has placed a growing emphasis on delivering measurable results. The rise of Results- Based Management (RBM) reflects this shift, as development actors seek to maximize impact, improve accountability, and ensure that limited re- sources are used effectively. However, while RBM has undoubtedly im- proved the design and monitoring of development programs, it has also generated an overwhelming volume of data, reports, and evaluations that are challenging to synthesize and apply effectively. Reports often remain static documents rather than evolving into dynamic learning tools that can guide future strategies. This raises an important question: how do we move beyond managing for results to managing the knowledge generated from these efforts? (The rest omitted.)

detail.title: Fostering Sustainable Lifestyles for Posterity
detail.abstract: The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development envisages harmony between humanity and nature towards the ideal of Sustainable Development. Achieving this ideal requires creating and maintaining the conditions under which humanity and nature can exist in productive harmony to support present and future generations. One of the key ways through which this ideal can be realized is by humanity embracing sustainable lifestyles in harmony with nature. This paper critically examines the need to embrace sustainable lifestyles. The paper defines the idea of sustainable lifestyles and argues that it is an urgent priority in the wake of global challenges including the triple planetary crisis of climate change, loss of biodiversity, and pollution. The paper explores some of the techniques that can be adopted towards fostering sustainable lifestyles for posterity.

detail.abstract:
The U.S. healthcare system faces two converging crises: the administrative inefficiency of a 50-state regulatory patchwork and the unregulated deployment of Artificial Intelligence (AI) to automate claim denials. This legislative white paper proposes the "Federal Algorithmic Insurance & Regulation (FAIR) Act," a comprehensive framework that establishes an Optional Federal Charter (OFC) for health insurers while mandating strict pre-market oversight for clinical AI.

The proposed framework functions as an "FDA for Algorithms," establishing a Federal Algorithmic Safety Board (FASB) funded by industry user fees (modeled on FDA MDUFA V). Key provisions include: (1) Mandatory "Stress Testing" of denial algorithms for clinical validity and racial bias prior to deployment; (2) A "Digital Custody" regime utilizing cryptographic hashing to prevent model drift; (3) Strict executive criminal liability for fraudulent safety certification; and (4) A "Grand Bargain" tax structure that creates federal regulatory efficiency while holding state budgets harmless. This proposal offers a deficit-neutral pathway to modernize insurance regulation and protect patients from the era of "Black Box" algorithmic denials.

title: A Unified Testing Approach for Risk Spillover based on RELTCoV
affiliations: Fudan University and Fudan University - School of Data Science

detail.title: A Unified Testing Approach for Risk Spillover based on RELTCoV
detail.abstract: Detecting risk spillovers is a critical research task, because accurate early warnings give regulators and risk managers the information they need to stop isolated shocks from spreading through the financial system. Developing flexible statistical methods for examining risk spillovers holds both theoretical and practical significance. This paper enhances the conventional CoVaR-based risk spillover test by introducing RELTCoV-the risk-equivalent level transition between CoVaR and VaR. RELTCoV identifies the balance point for the equivalence between CoVaR and VaR. After establishing existence and uniqueness, we embed RELTCoV in a joint test for multi-asset risk spillovers. Our approach turns out a generalized framework of testing risk spillover effects for a class of CoVaR measures. Moreover, we construct the test statistic coupling non-parametric RELT-CoV estimators with a bootstrap covariance matrix, and the asymptotic propoerties are derived. Finally, simulations reveal superior size and power, and an empirical exercise confirms practical usefulness.

title: Local energy market business models: A comparative study of theory to practical deployments
affiliations: University of Bristol - Department of Computer Science, , , Centre for Environment and Sustainability - University of Surrey, The University of Manchester, ,  and University of Glasgow

detail.title: Local energy market business models: A comparative study of theory to practical deployments
detail.abstract: The recent interest in local energy systems and distributed energy business models has led to a proliferation of academic publications on peer-to-peer, transactive, and community self-consumption local energy business models, and to the deployment of practical pilot projects that implement these approaches. This article presents a comparative study of deployed local energy market projects versus the typology of business models derived from the academic literature. It highlights what the practical deployment projects have adapted from the theoretical business model typologies, where they differ, and observes the reasons for such divergences. Among other findings, we observe that all case studies and pilot projects in practice fall within a combination of two or more business model archetypes identified in the theoretical literature. This is most often caused by regulatory constraints and/or in pursuit of opportunities for additional revenue streams. Other common divergences between theory and practice include the need in practice to account for participant preferences beyond financial concerns, the ability of certain stakeholders to assume multiple roles within a business model, the absence of community-building functions in theoretical business models, along with their lack of integration of regulatory and physical constraints.Policy implications of such divergences are also considered, along with recommendations for key stakeholders to allow  successful deployment of future local energy projects.

detail.abstract: This study describes students' adaptive reasoning abilities in solving HOTs type questions in Kolb's learning style. The method used to determine students' adaptive reasoning ability in solving HOTS (Higher Order Thinking Skill) uses qualitative research with a descriptive approach and type questions regarding learning styles (diverger, assimilator, converger, and accommodator types). The research subjects were thirty-five students of class XI. The results of data analysis and discussion can be concluded that students of class XI MIPS-3 SMA Negeri 4 Pasuruan have adaptive reasoning abilities in solving solutions to the HOTS type questions through the Polya step in terms of Kolb's learning style. Students who have adaptive reasoning ability solve the HOTS type problem solving through the Polya step in terms of Kolb's learning style. Students with a converger type of learning style can meet all indicators of adaptive reasoning ability (propose conjectures or conjectures, provide reasons or evidence about the truth of a statement, draw conclusions from an idea, check the validity of an argument, and find patterns from a mathematical problem) and all indicators in the Polya step (understand the problem, make a plan, implement the plan and reexamine the results).

detail.abstract:
This research unveils a critical thermodynamic law governing development finance: financial energy is subject to irreversible entropy generation, systematically dissipating within governance systems before conversion into public goods. Challenging conventional aid models, we demonstrate that the core problem is not merely the volume of funding but the efficiency of its conversion, a dimension largely ignored in prior literature. Our groundbreaking empirical analysis, using an original global panel dataset, yields three transformative observations. First, we establish a new metric for "irreversible loss," revealing an average 35% efficiency gap in WASH sectors. Second, we provide causal evidence that democratic accountability is not a mere correlate but a powerful moderator, with a significant positive interaction effect (β = 0.029, p < 0.05) showing that finance only achieves its potential in accountable systems. Third, we document this phenomenon in both composite efficiency and physical infrastructure, demonstrating that democracy reduces physical water loss (β = -1.842, p < 0.05). These findings fundamentally redefine aid effectiveness, shifting the paradigm from conditional input-outcome models to a thermodynamic theory of political conversion efficiency. The policy implication is revolutionary: without concomitant investment in democratic accountability, a significant portion of global development finance is thermodynamically destined for dissipation, irrevocably lost to its human development goals.
Keywords: Irreversible Loss, Entropy, Democratic Accountability, Conversion Efficiency, Development Finance, WASH, Thermodynamic Model, Causal Inference.

title: The Structural Current Account Deficits of Emerging Market Economies: Trade, Income and Transfers
affiliations: Wellesley College - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Structural Current Account Deficits of Emerging Market Economies: Trade, Income and Transfers
detail.abstract: The current accounts of most emerging economies include primary income deficits, which in turn largely consist of investment income payments on foreign direct investment earnings. For these countries, the persistent deficits have become a structural component of the current account. In addition, for some countries secondary income, which includes personal transfers from workers who are abroad, is also crucial. These surpluses partly offset the deficits in trade and primary income. We examine the response of the trade balance, primary income and secondary income balances to macroeconomic factors in a sample of 24 emerging markets economics over the period of 1990-2022. We use seemingly unrelated regressions models with random effects to account for correlated errors across the three equations and compare these results with the results of an estimate of the current account. The responses of the three subbalances to policy and control variables varies widely, which can complicate efforts to lower a current account deficit. We examine the response of the three sub-balances to financial crises, which increase the current and trade accounts. We also discuss the use of retained earnings to finance new FDI.

detail.abstract: Climate adaptation repeatedly fails not because nations lack funding, but because the capital systems used to finance adaptation are misaligned with the physical and temporal dynamics of climate risk. Using Regenerative Cycle Architecture (RCA)—a general theory of multi-cycle, non-liability capital for fragility-dominated systems—this paper shows that climate adaptation is governed by a political fragility cycle in which short electoral cycles override the long, recurring lifetimes of climate assets. Traditional capital instruments—grants, debt, insurance, and annual public budgets—are single-cycle or liability-bearing systems, structurally incompatible with adaptation’s multi-cycle mission demands. We define PSC-G (Perpetual Social Capital – Governance Mode) as the political-mode instantiation of PSC within RCA. PSC-G does not operate as a financial instrument; it functions as a capital constitution that separates capital cycles from political cycles , ensuring that pumps, levees, coastal buffers, cooling centres, fire equipment, and drought infrastructure are replaced predictably and transparently across government turnover. PSC-G provides zero-liability, shock-tolerant capital continuity; enforces rule-based replacement windows; embeds cross-cycle institutional memory; and prevents silent deferral, the dominant cause of catastrophic climate failure. At the national scale, PSC-G Climate Pools stabilise adaptation across regions and administrations, providing LGAs with autonomous, multi-decade capital cycles while preserving fiscal neutrality and eliminating sovereign fragility. For developing nations, PSC-G replaces disaster-driven borrowing with sovereign-safe cycle governance, and enables federated regional PSC-G pools that reduce dependency on volatile donor and insurance cycles. Extending PSC-G globally, we propose a Global Regenerative Climate Fund (GRCF) : a federated, cycle-governed, zero-liability capital architecture that provides the institutional substrate missing from COP21, the Green Climate Fund, and other global climate finance mechanisms. Our central argument is that climate adaptation does not require more capital—it requires capital that behaves differently . PSC-G is the first architecture that aligns capital behaviour with the physical and political realities of a world of recurring and intensifying climate shocks.

title: Centralized vs. Decentralized markets with Cash and Equity: Experimental Evidence
affiliations: BI Norwegian Business School, University of Stavanger and University of Stavanger

detail.title: Centralized vs. Decentralized markets with Cash and Equity: Experimental Evidence
detail.abstract: We investigate how market formats and payment structures under asymmetric information impact seller revenues. Our environment varies (i) market format between decentralized and centralized, and (ii) payment structure between equity and cash. In the decentralized format, the seller sets the terms of trade and is randomly matched with a potential buyer. In contrast, the centralized format involves buyers bidding and competing in pairs, similar to an auction. We find that while contingent payments help achieve higher revenues in decentralized markets relative to cash payments, seller revenues are highest in the centralized market with cash payments. Contrary to theory, adverse selection hinders the success of centralized markets with contingent payments.

detail.abstract:
This paper constitutes the third installment in The Republic’s Conscience doctrinal series and operates in direct tandem with its companion framework, The Interagency Integrity Doctrine: A National-Security Framework for Statutory Clarity and Bureaucratic Coherence. Together, these works articulate a unified architecture for understanding how legal precision and institutional compartmentalization preserve the functional integrity of the American Republic. The Structural Silo Doctrine (SSD) advances this project by establishing the first comprehensive constitutional, statutory, and institutional theory that reconceives agency silos not as bureaucratic inefficiencies, but as essential structural components of the constitutional order. In contrast to modern assumptions that view silos as administrative obstacles, SSD demonstrates that agency boundaries function as intra-executive counterparts to separation of powers: they preserve clarity of function, prevent authority fusion, protect decision-architecture, and safeguard continuity of government.

Drawing on Article I delegation principles, Article II supervisory doctrines, the Appropriations Clause, the non-delegation lineage from J.W. Hampton to Gundy, and the post-Chevron administrative landscape, the doctrine argues that ambiguous statutory drafting—particularly when it collapses or overlaps substantive agency mandates—forces the President to resolve jurisdictional contradictions that Congress alone is constitutionally empowered to clarify. This inversion of Article I–II logic burdens the Executive with adjudicative obligations it was never designed to bear, producing systemic incoherence that threatens national security as directly as regulatory misalignment. Through comparative administrative analysis, SSD demonstrates that stable governments—whether parliamentary, civil-law, or hybrid—rely on explicit competence doctrines to maintain governance coherence. The United States, lacking such an explicit doctrine, must articulate one. SSD provides that missing framework.

The Doctrine further aligns with national-security jurisprudence by showing that foreign intelligence services routinely exploit statutory ambiguity, fragmented jurisdiction, and executive-branch overload as vectors of institutional destabilization. Thus, structural clarity is not merely a matter of administrative precision; it is a form of constitutional defense.

Ultimately, The Structural Silo Doctrine reframes silos as constitutional infrastructure—boundaries that protect lawful delegation, preserve institutional identity, and anchor the Executive’s ability to govern coherently under both normal and crisis conditions. By supplying Congress, agencies, and the courts with a reproducible constitutional framework for drafting, interpreting, and enforcing structural boundaries, SSD restores the conditions under which the separation of powers can function continuously, predictably, and securely. It is a doctrine of preservation: shielding the Republic not by expanding power, but by restoring the structural clarity that makes power governable.

title: The Law on The Transnational Sales Contracts in Bangladesh – Need for Harmonisation
affiliations: Metropolitan University, Sylhet, Bangladesh

detail.title: The Law on The Transnational Sales Contracts in Bangladesh – Need for Harmonisation
detail.abstract: The contract and the governance of the contract form the foundational element of international trade. It, therefore, requires an effective legal regime that performs a dual purpose—ensures the efficient and effective performance of the contracts and seamlessly interacts with other international legal regimes that impact the contract. Bangladesh is faced with legal roadblocks in its quest to promote seamless interaction and facilitation of performance in transnational contracts. The law impacting transnational contracts as it exists now is found in different laws that are neither conceived for regulating these contracts nor have sufficient legal strength to facilitate the performance of contracts. This doctoral research aims to identify and articulate the concerns within the law related to the governance of transnational contracts in Bangladesh. After outlining the concerns within the existing law(s), the thesis attempts to make a few suggestions for law reform and pleads for accession to harmonized legal regimes. Transnational commerce has multiple points of interaction and, therefore, a multitude of contracts referencing the main contract. However, this research is related to Bangladesh's transnational sales contracts law regime. The research focuses only on the existing transnational sales contracts law and harmonise the sales contracts' laws. This research will exclude contracts related to service, labour, property, insurance, etc., and consumer protection issues.

title: Automation, Fragmentation, and Changes in Comparative Advantage
affiliations: University of California, San Diego (UCSD)

detail.title: Automation, Fragmentation, and Changes in Comparative Advantage
detail.abstract: Comparative advantage is the backbone of international trade, but little is known about its changes over time. First, I empirically show that developing countries used to have a comparative advantage in low-skill-intensive industries, but this relationship has weakened since the late 1990s and has disappeared after the 2000s. This decoupling of skills and comparative advantage is particularly present in sectors exposed to automation and fragmentation or countries that adopt automation. Second, I develop a simple theoretical framework and characterize the effect of automation and fragmentation on changes in comparative advantage. Automation and fragmentation of production processes allow developed countries to rely on machines or foreign labor, making domestic skill endowments less important in comparative advantage. Finally, I develop a quantitative trade model with automation and fragmentation to quantify the importance of the mechanism and draw implications for structural change and welfare. I demonstrate the greater importance of automation in changing comparative advantage and illustrate that developing countries would have specialized in manufacturing sectors without automation. Automation disproportionally improves the welfare of developed countries while fragmentation benefits countries more equally.

title: Assessing The United Arab Emirates' Institutional and Investment Frameworks to Catalyse the Renewable Energy Transition
affiliations: Shanghai International Studies University, University of Qom and Payam-e-Noor University

detail.title: Assessing The United Arab Emirates' Institutional and Investment Frameworks to Catalyse the Renewable Energy Transition
detail.abstract: Amid accelerating climate change, persistent global energy security concerns, and the imperative to provide sustainable and affordable energy for all, the expansion of renewable energy has become a universal priority. Yet the widespread adoption of renewables demands substantial financial and technological investment—resources that many states, particularly in the developing world, cannot mobilise independently. This reality underscores the critical importance of promoting foreign investment in the renewable energy sector, especially in light of the limited success of international initiatives to date. Amongst a handful of states that have assumed leadership in the global energy transition, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) has emerged as a frontrunner—not only within the Gulf Cooperation Council but across the broader developing world. Since the early 2000s, the UAE has pursued ambitious policies aimed at deploying renewable energy technologies both domestically and internationally. This article seeks to address a central question: what factors have enabled the UAE to emerge as a regional pioneer in renewable energy development, and in what ways is it contributing to the global energy transition? Employing a qualitative methodology, the study explores the UAE’s renewable energy development trajectory. The findings reveal that the State’s institutional architecture, its regulatory and investment frameworks—both national and foreign— and its commitment to fostering international partnerships constitute the core pillars of its energy transition strategy. The article concludes by identifying key practices with broader relevance for policymakers, international negotiators, and academics engaged in the global energy and climate governance discourse.

title: Representing the Incommunicado Client: Regulating the Attorney-Client Relationship in a Civil Rights Emergency
affiliations: University of Nevada, Las Vegas, William S. Boyd School of Law

detail.title: Representing the Incommunicado Client: Regulating the Attorney-Client Relationship in a Civil Rights Emergency
detail.abstract: When the government obstructs a detainee’s ability to communicate with attorneys, normal rules governing the formation of attorney-client relationships break down. While some work-arounds exist to allow lawyers to bring such cases to court, they have significant limitations and can create problems of their own. The legal profession and the courts should adopt new rules modeled on emergency medicine to facilitate the filing of urgent civil rights claims  or clients who are not in a position to consent. In emergency medicine, physicians can presume client consent for certain narrow and urgent purposes. Certain lawyers, in extreme cases, should be able to do the same.

title: Informational Feedback and ESG Growth Opportunities: Optimal Public Disclosure
affiliations: and ESADE Business School

detail.title: Informational Feedback and ESG Growth Opportunities: Optimal Public Disclosure
detail.abstract: We develop a rational expectations model to study the optimal precision of firm's public disclosure when traders have heterogeneous preferences and the firm learns from market prices to guide its ESG investment decisions. In our model, the firm’s payoff combines financial and ESG components, while traders differ in the component they value. The firm's manager can publicly disclose noisy signals about these components and uses stock prices to infer the value of an ESG-linked growth opportunity. We show that when the manager's private information is imprecise, the investment opportunity is large, and prices are more informative about the value of the ESG component that the manager wants to learn about, greater precision of public disclosure may impair firm’s ability to learn from prices and may reduce firm value. In contrast, when manager's information is highly precise, the investment opportunity is small, and prices are more informative about the financial component, full disclosure increases firm value. Thus, the firms' optimal disclosure policy balances the benefits of price efficiency against the costs of reduced market-based learning, generating a non-monotonic relationship between disclosure and firm value. Our findings uncover novel trade-offs in public disclosure design and offer policy implications for firms and policymakers navigating evolving transparency mandates. JEL codes: G11; G20; G23.

title: House Prices, Quantities, and the Propagation of Shocks when Developers Are Imperfectly Competitive
affiliations: University of British Columbia (UBC) - Division of Finance, Finance Division, Sauder School of Business, University of British Columbia (UBC) and University of British Columbia (UBC) - Division of Finance

detail.title: House Prices, Quantities, and the Propagation of Shocks when Developers Are Imperfectly Competitive
detail.abstract: We create a novel dataset identifying the quantity, location, and timing of home sales by national and local U.S. developers in order to study concentration in housing construction markets. Smaller markets and more regulated markets are more concentrated, suggesting the importance of fixed entry or operating costs. Concentration matters, with more concentrated CBSAs having higher prices and lower quantities. Negative price shocks originating in one CBSA cause developers to shrink or exit other markets, thus propagating through the CBSA-developer network, reducing competition and raising prices in connected CBSAs. These patterns provide new evidence on how imperfect competition in housing construction and financial frictions propagate local housing shocks across space.

title: Strategic Annexation Without Occupation: The Political Economy Nexus of Trumpism and Neo-Colonial Resource Geopolitics in Africa
affiliations: The Integrity Organisation Ltd. (gte.)

detail.title: Strategic Annexation Without Occupation: The Political Economy Nexus of Trumpism and Neo-Colonial Resource Geopolitics in Africa

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not Applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: NIL

detail.abstract: This paper examines an emerging geopolitical scenario in which Donald Trump’s return to the U.S. presidency amid global economic instability, the erosion of multilateral institutions, and the ascent of extractive techno-industrial elites positions Africa as a focal point in a new resource scramble. Using a qualitative methodology grounded in critical political economy, strategic foresight, and postcolonial analysis, the paper explores how techno-state alliances and a potential U.S.–Russia rapprochement could accelerate a neo-colonial dynamic centred on Africa’s critical minerals, including lithium, cobalt, iridium, and rare earth elements. The analysis argues that Africa’s structural vulnerabilities, deepened by sovereign debt dependence, pervasive corruption, elite capture, and institutional fragility, expose it to extractive partnerships disguised as development cooperation. Drawing on Trump’s prior territorial rhetoric concerning Greenland, Panama, and Canada, and recent threats to invade Nigeria, the study anticipates a model of “strategic annexation” without formal occupation implemented through contracts, coercion, and elite complicity. The paper contributes to debates in political economy on authoritarian realignment, resource sovereignty, and Africa’s role in a multipolar global order. It concludes with strategic recommendations for African regional institutions, civil society actors, and Global South coalitions to defend sovereignty and forestall a new cycle of mineral dependency.

title: Chinese Imports and Industrialization in Africa: Evidence from Ethiopia
affiliations: Tufts University

detail.title: Chinese Imports and Industrialization in Africa: Evidence from Ethiopia
detail.abstract: The rise of Chinese exports has transformed trade dynamics globally, often harming manufacturing employment in high- and middle-income countries through import competition. However, the impact in low-income countries remains unclear, particularly where access to high-quality intermediate inputs is limited. This paper analyzes the effect of Chinese import penetration on manufacturing employment in Ethiopia, decomposing the impacts into competition and input channels using input-output tables. Imports of intermediate goods from China are found to lead to significant increases in manufacturing employment, largely through productivity gains and higher capacity utilization, while final goods imports show no detectable effect. These results suggest that reducing barriers to imported intermediates can support industrialization and jobcreation in low-income economies with underdeveloped supply chains. The findings suggest that easing barriers to intermediate imports can foster industrialization and job creation.

title: Exploring the Nexus of Intellectual Capital and Human Development for Sustainable Competitiveness in Southeast Asia
affiliations: Universitas Muhammadiyah Purwokerto, Universitas Muhammadiyah Purwokerto,  and Universitas Muhammadiyah Purwokerto

detail.title: Exploring the Nexus of Intellectual Capital and Human Development for Sustainable Competitiveness in Southeast Asia
detail.abstract: The role of intellectual capital in fostering human development has become central in the knowledge economy, yet the extent to which national intellectual capital (NIC) drives sustainable outcomes remains underexplored. This study examines the impact of NIC on the Human Development Index (HDI) across Southeast Asian countries from 2002 to 2023. Using balanced panel data, two models are estimated: the first explores the aggregate influence of NIC on HDI, while the second disaggregates NIC into human, structural, and relational capital to capture their distinct effects. Panel regression with fixed effects controls for country-specific heterogeneity, and Driscoll–Kraay robust standard errors correct for heteroskedasticity, autocorrelation, and cross-sectional dependence. The results show that NIC positively and significantly affects HDI, confirming the pivotal role of knowledge-based assets in promoting sustainable human development. All three components—human, structural, and relational capital—also exhibit significant positive effects, reflecting how education, health, institutional quality, technological capacity, and international linkages collectively enhance development outcomes. Control variables such as GDP per capita, trade openness, and inflation further shape HDI. Overall, the study underscores NIC as a key determinant of sustainable human growth in Southeast Asia, providing policy insights for aligning knowledge-based strategies with long-term development and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

title: New Varieties of Plants and Legal Protection of Breeder’s Right – the UPOV Convention and its Major Economic Consequences
affiliations: and

detail.title: New Varieties of Plants and Legal Protection of Breeder’s Right – the UPOV Convention and its Major Economic Consequences
detail.abstract: The International Convention for the Protection of New Varieties of Plants (UPOV Convention) represents the most comprehensive international legal mechanism in this field. In spite of the fact that the UPOV Convention introduces only certain minimal common rules regarding the so called breeder's right, the efficiency and the level of acceptance of the entire UPOV system have had numerous economic and social benefits: significant increase of productivity, transparent and just mechanism for rewarding scientific effort and investment in research, important incentive for international trade of new varieties of plants and undisputed impact on agricultural and horticultural development. This paper provides a targeted analysis of the important provisions of the UPOV convention (notion of breeder, grant of breeder's right and its content) and examines some of its major economic consequences. It argues that the UPOV convention remains an effective international legal mechanism for the protection of new varieties of plants.

title: Beyond Rhetoric: Structural Barriers, Social License, and the Future of Gender-Inclusive Sustainable Finance
affiliations: Externado de Colombia University

detail.title: Beyond Rhetoric: Structural Barriers, Social License, and the Future of Gender-Inclusive Sustainable Finance
detail.abstract:
This chapter aims to critically analyze the intersection of gender allocation, constitutional frameworks, and sustainable finance. We challenge the idea that economic inclusivity and gender equality are the natural result of market innovation and progressive policy, especially in the context of sustainable finance. Our analysis seeks to identify that structural barriers within the functioning of financial systems might often perpetuate exclusion, raising questions about whether current sustainable finance models truly promote inclusion or simply mask or are being designed to hide existing disparities under a new label.

The query is to assess whether financial services offer fair outcomes for everyone by examining impact investing and related mechanisms, and their roles, if any, in addressing gender imbalance or maintaining the status quo. By exploring case studies, we seek to highlight how gender-focused initiatives can either promote real, transformative empowerment or serve as performative compliance with ESG standards.

To strengthen these points, we adopt the concept of social license coined by David Rausch, emphasizing the importance of re-evaluating the legitimacy of financial actors. Instead of relying on policy statements or superficial metrics, this approach values relationships built through ongoing, participatory engagement with marginalized and excluded communities. Therefore, the question is whether gender-sensitive policies alone are sufficient, or whether genuine dialogue with affected groups and active efforts to challenge institutional biases are necessary to build trust and legitimacy.

In order to provide the framework for these arguments, we advocate in favour of seeing transformative constitutionalism as essential to genuine inclusion. We suggest that comprehensive institutional reform is a prerequisite for meaningful progress, calling for policies that go beyond the sometimes-rhetorical promises and embed gender equality into legal, financial, and constitutional structures. Furthermore, we analyze the roots of resistance to reform, illustrating how cultural opposition and what can be identified as institutional inertia sustain disadvantages. Power relations and institutional inertia influence how gender finance is implemented. The analysis presented in this chapter also helps us to argue in favour of the importance of continuous empirical research and thorough evaluation, ensuring impact assessments or regulatory reforms go beyond headline figures to explore the systemic roots of exclusion.

Finally, the chapter argues for a paradigm shift that is expected to change the way we understand the purpose behind certain parts of sustainable finance. This is to understand that gender equity must be recognized as a fundamental principle and a core component of both sustainable finance and constitutional reform. In this context, there is a need to promote and enhance interdisciplinary engagement among policymakers, legal experts, scholars, economic actors, and civil society, which is crucial to developing evidence-based solutions capable of dismantling and breaking down persistent exclusion.

title: Government Spending, Income Distribution, and Productivity Enhancing *
affiliations: Goethe University Frankfurt

detail.title: Government Spending, Income Distribution, and Productivity Enhancing *
detail.abstract: This paper examines the distributional and innovation effects of fiscal spending. Using data for 154 countries from 1980 to 2023, I show that expansionary government spending persistently raises output and total factor productivity up to more than 10 years while compressing income inequality. Under sanctions, the productivity effect of government spending is stronger when private sector resources are constrained, which amplifies the innovation response. Countries with a higher share of inclusive spending further intensify the inequality-reducing impact. A standard two-agent New Keynesian model with endogenous growth and productive public investment rationalizes the evidence and matches the dynamic responses, linking innovation-driven TFP gains to persistent output effects and distributional improvements.

title: Architectures of Ease: A Theory of Enforcement-Free Compliance in Regenerative Capital Systems

detail.title: Architectures of Ease: A Theory of Enforcement-Free Compliance in Regenerative Capital Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. This research was conducted independently as part of the Institute of Regenerative Systems Architecture (IRSA) theoretical research program. No commercial, financial, or personal relationships influenced the development of this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study, as it involves no human participants, no personal data, and no experimental interventions. This paper develops a theoretical behavioural-systems model and does not include empirical human-subject research.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this research. The work was undertaken as part of the IRSA independent research program without financial support from any public or private sponsor.

detail.abstract: Traditional financial and institutional systems rely on enforcement—contracts, penalties, surveillance, and coercive compliance—to ensure participation. This paper introduces Architectures of Ease, a unified behavioural-systems theory explaining how pro-social compliance can emerge without enforcement when systems are designed such that desired behaviours are easier, more rewarding, and more identity-aligned than defection. Drawing on behavioural economics, platform design, commons governance, and systems theory, we argue that people do not rise to the level of their moral values; they fall to the level of the systems they inhabit. We formalise three mechanisms—friction differentials, identity-coupled participation, and future-cycle access—that create self-reinforcing compliance equilibria in regenerative systems. We demonstrate how ease-based architectures underpin non-extractive capital mechanisms such as Perpetual Social Capital (PSC), alignment operators (Λ, Δ), and regenerative cycle design (RCA). By reframing compliance as an emergent systems property rather than a function of enforcement, this paper offers a general behavioural foundation for the design of institutions, capital systems, and digital infrastructures capable of producing durable, regenerative, and non-coercive participation.

title: The (Hidden) Samaritan Contest
affiliations: Center for Natural Resource Studies (CNRS), , University of Oxford and

detail.title: The (Hidden) Samaritan Contest
detail.abstract: This paper explores whether foreign aid is driven by a (hidden) contest amongst donors to access natural resources, exploiting the timing and size of major mineral discoveries. We first analyze the effect a resource discovery in a two-by-two donor-recipient model with an altruistic motive of donors vis-à-vis recipients alongside (an otherwise hidden) conflict about natural resources, using a contest success function.  We then estimate the effects of major discoveries using a gravity model for a large panel of countries. Results show that recipient countries that experience major discoveries receive more, not less, bilateral aid. Our main result is not directly but rather indirectly driven by China which entry in the World Trade Organization in 2001 heightened the global competition for access to natural resources. We conclude that the energy transition and its requirement in minerals will further exacerbate the (hidden) contest amongst aid donors.

title: Regulation versus Courts: The Equity Market's View
affiliations: Australian National University (ANU), Monash University and Macquarie University, Macquarie Business School

detail.title: Regulation versus Courts: The Equity Market's View

declarations.declarationOfInterest: there are no conflict of interests from any of the Authors
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: Smith has funding from ARC Discovery Grant DP220102985

detail.abstract: We examine how financial markets value regulation versus courts as enforcement mechanisms by exploiting the Supreme Court's 2024 reversal of Chevron deference, which shifted interpretive authority from federal agencies to the judiciary. Using firm-level event studies, we document substantial cross-sectional heterogeneity in abnormal returns: heavily regulated firms and medium-sized firms gain, while small firms experience significant losses. These effects are amplified in districts with congested or ideologically imbalanced courts. We further show that judicialization increases volatility and downside tail risk, particularly for small firms. Our findings indicate that markets view regulation as costly but courts as uncertain, revealing a trade-off in governance structures that differentially affects firms.

title: The Political Economy of Femicides: Local Spending Responses, Electoral Incentives and Nationality Bias
affiliations: University of Bergamo - Department of Economics, University of Bergamo and University of Calabria

detail.title: The Political Economy of Femicides: Local Spending Responses, Electoral Incentives and Nationality Bias

declarations.funderStatement: This study was funded by the European Union - NextGenerationEU, in the framework of the GRINS - Growing Resilient, INclusive and Sustainable project (GRINS PE00000018 – CUP F83C22001720001). The views and opinions expressed are solely those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect those of the European Union, nor can the European Union be held responsible for them. Moreover, this work was funded by the Εuropean Union – NextGenerationEU, under the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (NRRP), Mission 4, Component 2, Investment 1.1, funding call PRIN 2022 D.D. 104 published on 2.2.2022 by the Italian Ministry of University and Research (Ministero dell’Università e della Ricerca), Project Title: BREAK THE BIAS: new data and methods to investigate the presence and impact of gender stereotypes on economic outcomes – CUP F53D23003020006.

detail.abstract: We study how local governments adjust fiscal policy following extreme acts of gender-based violence, and whether these adjustments are shaped by migration-related concerns. Combining administrative data on femicides with municipal budgets for Italian municipalities, we exploit femicides as shocks to the local salience of violence in staggered difference-indifferences models. Femicides trigger a sizable and persistent increase in security expenditures, concentrated on local police, with little corresponding expansion of prevention-oriented or social services for women at risk. The magnitude and persistence of the security response depend strongly on the perpetrator's nationality: when the perpetrator is foreign-born, the increase in police spending is much larger and more persistent. These patterns are consistent with high-profile crimes involving foreigners being more likely to be politicized and framed as public-order threats, reallocating scarce local resources toward visible security measures and away from policies more directly targeted at reducing gender-based violence.

title: The Impact of Climate Change on Reserves in Life Insurance
affiliations: Vienna University of Economics and Business - Department of Finance, Accounting & Statistics and Macquarie University - Department of Actuarial Studies and Business Analytics

detail.title: The Impact of Climate Change on Reserves in Life Insurance
detail.abstract: Climate change poses serious challenges to various sectors of the economy, including the insurance industry. One important channel for this impact is through mortality rates, which directly affect the financial reserves of life insurers. Accurately assessing this relationship is essential for ensuring the sustainability and solvency of life insurance portfolios. In this study, we present a framework for incorporating climate risk into the stress testing of life insurers' reserves. Using temperature projections generated from a stochastic version of the DICE cost-benefit integrated assessment model, we simulate mortality shocks driven by changes in global mean temperature and evaluate their impact on pricing and reserving for life insurance and life annuity policies. Our numerical analysis demonstrates that ignoring climate risk can lead to material mispricing of premiums and reveals notable differences in reserve requirements, thereby highlighting the importance of integrating climate risk into actuarial modeling and financial planning for life insurers.

title: Long-Term Simulation of the Day-Ahead Electricity Market Towards a Fully Decarbonized Economy
affiliations: RWTH Aachen University and RWTH Aachen University

detail.title: Long-Term Simulation of the Day-Ahead Electricity Market Towards a Fully Decarbonized Economy
detail.abstract:
Day-ahead markets for electricity are important institutions in modern energy systems, but their
functioning in a future, decarbonized economy has not yet been fully clarified. We address this
question with a stochastic long-term simulation for the German market, in which intermittent
renewable power generation and total electricity demand are modeled with separate stochastic
processes. Model precision is achieved by using mean-reverting processes with time-dependent
trend functions and positive dynamics that are calibrated to the current market. Model robustness
is ensured by emulating a large number of different scenarios taken from recent research on a
sustainable energy transition in Germany. The simulation shows that in a completely decarbonized
economy, the day-ahead market for electricity continues to function: the price formation still
works, the price volatility is increasing only moderately, and the electricity price remains sufficient
for recovering capital investment. Consequently, the current energy-only market does not need to
be complemented with capacity-oriented mechanisms. The long-term simulation further informs
on the cost effectiveness of certain aspects of the ongoing sustainable energy transition, which is
an important contribution to current policy. The model provides a suitable basis for future work
with other stochastic methods like real options analysis, and it can be generalized to other markets.

title: Fundamental Rights in Out-of-Court Dispute Settlement under the Digital Services Act
affiliations: Universität Osnabrück - Faculty of Law and University of Amsterdam - Institute for Information Law (IViR)

detail.title: Fundamental Rights in Out-of-Court Dispute Settlement under the Digital Services Act
detail.abstract: This paper argues that certified out-of-court dispute settlement (ODS) bodies under Article 21 of the Digital Services Act (DSA) should apply a structured fundamental rights review to platform content moderation, operationalised through the concept of case salience. Situating ODS within the DSA's broader regulatory architecture-particularly Articles 14(4), 17, and 20-the paper contends that Article 21 provides the procedural complement to Article 14(4)'s substantive duty to enforce terms of service "diligently, objectively and proportionately, with due regard to fundamental rights." Rather than extending the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union (CFR) horizontally in a direct sense, ODS bodies give effect to Charter-conforming statutory obligations owed by platforms, interpreted in light of Article 52(1) CFR. Drawing on jurisprudence from the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU), the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR), and national courts, the paper shows how freedom of expression and information interacts with countervailing rights-such as the freedom to conduct a business, privacy and data protection, and human dignity-in the context of online moderation. It proposes an intensity-of-review model: a deeper, meritsbased proportionality analysis for high-impact cases (e.g. political speech, account suspensions, issues of systemic relevance), and a lighter, procedural-sufficiency check for routine disputes. The paper emphasises that ODS remains non-judicial and operates without prejudice to Article 47 CFR and the availability of national court remedies. Over time, reasoned ODS decisions could evolve into a body of soft law, enhancing consistency and transparency in platform accountability. Ultimately, ODS bodies under the DSA represent a novel experiment in multi-actor rights protection. Their success will depend on whether they can reconcile accessibility, efficiency, and rights-based rigour, ensuring that content moderation in Europe evolves in line with the constitutional values of the Charter.

title: Quantile-Based Power-Series Expansions of the Johnson Distribution System
affiliations: University of Texas at Austin

detail.title: Quantile-Based Power-Series Expansions of the Johnson Distribution System
detail.abstract: The Johnson system of distributions provides a flexible framework for modeling continuous random variables through monotonic transformations of the standard normal distribution. Despite its widespread use, the system is typically presented in transformation form, which obscures the analytic structure of its quantile functions. This paper introduces a novel formulation: explicit power-series expansions for the Johnson SU, SL, and SB quantile functions, expressed in terms of a centered standard normal quantile function. These Johnson Power-Series Expansions (JPSE) provide a new analytic foundation for the Johnson system and facilitate structured quantile-based modeling. The SU and SB expansions consist of odd powers, but only SU has strictly positive coefficients, ensuring monotonicity for all truncation orders. In contrast, the SB expansion involves alternating-sign coefficients and may violate monotonicity under truncation. The SL expansion includes both even and odd powers with positive coefficients, requiring careful selection of truncation order to preserve validity. We derive convergence rates, remainder bounds, and sufficient conditions for monotonicity, and demonstrate through Q-Q and density comparisons that low-order truncations yield accurate approximations across the Johnson families. These results support the development of quantile-parameterized distribution systems for applications in expert elicitation and empirical quantile fitting.

title: The Migration Hypothesis of Financial Markets

detail.title: The Migration Hypothesis of Financial Markets
detail.abstract: Financial assets migrate. This proposition is set in a risk-return universe (RRU), defined by a 3×3 matrix of nine zones. I used a total of over 2.5 million daily price observations for 707 assets over ten years in this study. Empirical results confirm that financial instruments typically leave underperforming zones and migrate into risk-adjusted habitats. They avoid high-risk and low-return zones, while changing position, velocity, acceleration, and duration across the RRU. Zone migration is reasonably predictable at 37.64% accuracy. The phenomenological migration hypothesis (MH) reconciles competing paradigms in finance—evidently, markets are efficient (gravitationally attracted toward optimal RRU zones) and irrational (transient in their occupation of dominated zones). The high predictive accuracy, structural universality, and out-of-sample validation collectively provide a new theoretical lens for considering market dynamics.

title: Financialization or Modernization? REIT Ownership, Amenities, and Reinvestment in Supply-Constrained Markets

detail.title: Financialization or Modernization? REIT Ownership, Amenities, and Reinvestment in Supply-Constrained Markets
detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether Real Estate Investment Trust (REIT) ownership affects multifamily rental housing affordability and quality in supply-constrained gateway cities. Using a novel dataset of rental listings in the Greater Toronto Area, matched with over 700,000 building permits classified via Large Language Models (LLMs), we test for rent premiums associated with REITs. We find that raw rent differentials are entirely explained by superior building amenities, location, and property quality. To address identification concerns, we exploit the November 2018 policy shock that exempted new construction from rent controls, finding no evidence of strategic overpricing by REITs even in this unregulated segment. Instead, the data reveal a distinct "reinvestment channel": REIT-owned properties are significantly more likely to secure permits for capital improvements and green retrofits. The results suggest that REITs drive the modernization and decarbonization of aging multifamily rental stock without exerting upward pressure on rents once adjusted for quality.

title: Housing Deposit Channel of Monetary Policy and Housing Price Double-Dip
affiliations: and Sorbonne University

detail.title: Housing Deposit Channel of Monetary Policy and Housing Price Double-Dip
detail.abstract:
“Rising interest rates lead to a gradual decline in housing prices.”, a widely held belief; this paper challenges that conventional wisdom both theoretically and empirically by showing that sustained monetary tightening activates a novel
transmission mechanism, i.e., the housing deposit channel, which gives rise to a double-dip in housing prices: an initial decline upon impact, followed by a temporary rebound, and a subsequent second dip in the longer run. A general equilibrium model formalizes the theory behind this mechanism, and empirically, lag-augmented local projection estimation techniques, supported by extensive robustness checks, demonstrate that the patterns observed in the US data align with the theoretical model’s predictions. Our study investigates the effects of monetary policy on the housing market and reciprocally, how the housing market influences the efficacy of monetary policy, particularly in achieving inflation targeting objectives.

title: Explaining Risk-Adjusted Performance Using Vectors
affiliations: Georgetown University - McDonough School of Business and MIT

detail.title: Explaining Risk-Adjusted Performance Using Vectors
detail.abstract: Risk-adjusted performance theory equations are often dry and not always obvious to the reader who may be more visual. In this brief note, we try to expand on the idea of using graphical vector representations of finance concepts to display some simple themes in risk-adjusted performance with the goal of creating a new visual representation of the same ideas as this has not been done before. We use the M-cube risk-adjusted performance measure and Ambarish-Seigel luck versus skill measure to make this point. The key aspect to the vector representation is that portfolios can be represented as vectors (including portfolios of multiple assets), and the correlation parameter is a cosine. These two simple acknowledgments lead to very fascinating visual representations of previously published research and opens a new avenue to a field we call Vector Finance.

title: Contingency of Structures: Triggers and the Social Geography of Revolutionary Episodes in Iran 2017-2022
affiliations: Boston College, Boston College, Stony Brook University, University of Oklahoma and University of Oxford

detail.title: Contingency of Structures: Triggers and the Social Geography of Revolutionary Episodes in Iran 2017-2022
detail.abstract: What drives the uneven geographic spread of revolutionary episodes? While structural approaches emphasize pre-existing fault lines, contingency approaches highlight emergent processes. We synthesize these perspectives, arguing that specific triggers shape a revolutionary episode’s social geography by activating certain fault lines while leaving others dormant. Through a comparative analysis of three revolutionary episodes in Iran (2017–2022), each with a distinct trigger, we demonstrate how different triggers shape patterns of contention. Using event-history and spatial regression analysis of subnational protest data alongside socioeconomic and political variables, we show that a fuel price hike activated grievances in oil-producing areas, while a repressive event targeting a woman from an ethnic and religious minority mobilized protests in minority-populated districts. Our findings illustrate how triggers structure revolutionary mobilization, offering broader insights into the interaction between structural conditions and contingent events in contentious politics.

title: The Fight Against Greenwashing between Environmentalism, Corporate Sustainability and Consumer Protection: the EU’s Regulatory Framework and Some Regulatory Approaches in Central and Eastern Europe

detail.title: The Fight Against Greenwashing between Environmentalism, Corporate Sustainability and Consumer Protection: the EU’s Regulatory Framework and Some Regulatory Approaches in Central and Eastern Europe
detail.abstract: The discrepancy between, on the one hand, the issue of greenwashing in academic research and public discourse, and, on the other, the effectiveness of the regulatory framework applicable to it has become increasingly disturbing in recent years. While economic operators often surpass each other in creativity regarding various false or unverifiable environmental claims, both the EU and national legislators are struggling to adopt a more adaptable and effective regulatory framework. Moreover, the very notion of greenwashing is not always easy to define (Section 2), especially when it comes to the legislative efforts to combat it. In such a context, this article examines the issue of EU legislation in corporate sustainability reporting (Section 3) and consumer protection (Section 4) applicable to greenwashing, before analysing some major specificities in three countries of Central and Eastern Europe (Section 5). While the ongoing regulatory reforms in the EU regarding corporate sustainability reporting and consumer protection have still not produced their full effect, in national legal orders the issue of greenwashing is often more extensively addressed in legally non-binding acts adopted by self-regulatory bodies.

title: The Impact of the FISU Summer World University Games on Local Tourism Demand: Evidence from Chengdu, China
affiliations: University of Georgia, Chengdu University and University of Georgia

detail.title: The Impact of the FISU Summer World University Games on Local Tourism Demand: Evidence from Chengdu, China
detail.abstract: This paper examines the effect of the 2021 [2023] FISU Summer World University Games on local tourism demand in the host city of Chengdu, China. We use an extensive dataset of daily hotel occupancy data to determine the impact on city tourism before, during, and after the Games. Using time-series intervention analysis and fixed effects regression design, we find that the FISU games generate approximately 2,471 additional hotel rooms demanded. However, these gains are likely offset by reductions in hotel occupancy and revenue in the months following the Games. We find no evidence that the Games generate long-term changes in tourism to the city. This paper contributes to the existing economic impact of sporting events literature and extends on it by examining both the World University Games and the Chinese tourism industry.

title: Federated Edge Intelligence for Community Microgrids: Human-AI Collaboration for Energy Resilience in Low-Resource Settings
affiliations: Fourth Industrial Systems Corporation

detail.title: Federated Edge Intelligence for Community Microgrids: Human-AI Collaboration for Energy Resilience in Low-Resource Settings

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known financial or personal conflicts of interest that could have influenced the research, analysis, or conclusions presented in this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human subjects research requiring Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval. The simulation components rely solely on publicly available benchmark datasets, and the user study involved voluntary feedback from adult participants in a non-clinical, low-risk setting. All participants provided informed consent prior to taking part.
declarations.funderStatement: Self-Funded (most common for independent research) This research was fully self-funded by the author. No external grants or financial sponsors supported the study.

detail.abstract:
This paper presents a Federated Edge Intelligence framework designed to improve the reliability, resilience, and equity of community-scale microgrids. Microgrids play a crucial role in decarbonization and expanding energy access, but their operation is complicated by uncertainty in renewable generation, diverse load patterns, and limited connectivity—conditions that often exceed the capacity of human operators alone.

The proposed framework deploys lightweight AI agents at the grid edge that collaborate with human stakeholders to support decisions related to energy storage management, demand response, and islanding. The architecture integrates three core components:

  1. Local edge learning and prediction on low-power devices,

  2. Federated optimization across multiple microgrids without centralized data sharing, and

  3. Human-in-the-loop controls supported by explainable recommendations to build operator trust.

Designed specifically for low-resource and intermittently connected environments, the framework prioritizes data minimization, robustness, and participatory governance. Simulation results using open microgrid benchmarks show significant performance gains, including a 32% reduction in loss-of-load probability and 18–27% reduction in diesel generator reliance, all while maintaining reliability under bandwidth constraints.

A user study with 16 microgrid operators and community representatives found that the use of explainable edge agents improved trust and increased willingness to adopt AI assistance. Overall, the work demonstrates a practical socio-technical pathway for bringing “AI for All” to energy infrastructure serving vulnerable communities through the combined use of federated learning, edge intelligence, and human oversight.

title: How Housing Supply Expansions Reshape Cities
affiliations: University of Notre Dame - Mendoza College of Business, Erasmus School of Economics and UNC Kenan-Flagler Business School - Finance Area

detail.title: How Housing Supply Expansions Reshape Cities
detail.abstract: We study a large-scale policy relaxing residential land supply constraints near major Dutch cities in the mid-1990s. Land allocation was determined centrally and was unrelated to pre-policy local market dynamics. Using administrative data, we explore effects on housing, mobility, and labor markets. New supply attracted high-income individuals, primarily from nearby high-income neighborhoods, where house prices decreased. New supply also increased local employment in surrounding areas, especially in high-earning occupations. We develop a rich quantitative spatial equilibrium model and show that the impact of relaxing supply constraints on housing markets and welfare crucially depends on job reallocation and on in-migration flows.

title: Vertical Control and Retail Competition: Evidence from Consumer Battery Industry
affiliations: Business School, National University of Singapore and National University of Singapore (NUS), Department of Economics

detail.title: Vertical Control and Retail Competition: Evidence from Consumer Battery Industry
detail.abstract: This paper examines the impact of a vertical agreement between a downstream retailer and an upstream manufacturer in the context of the U.S. consumer battery industry, using detailed consumer receipt panel data. Following the agreement between Walmart (the retailer) and Energizer (the manufacturer), Walmart increases the retail prices of Duracell, Energizer's main competitor, while Energizer increases the wholesale prices charged to other retailers competing with Walmart. We document a shift in Walmart's sales from Duracell toward Energizer and retail price increases of about 6-7 percent for both brands across major retailers. To interpret these patterns, we estimate a model of consumer demand and retailer-manufacturer bargaining that treats Walmart and Energizer as an integrated party in the post-agreement period. Counterfactual analyses show that Duracell, though not part of the agreement, benefits from higher prices. Moreover, when similar agreements involve smaller retailers, they induce even larger wholesale and retail price increases elsewhere, resulting in greater consumer harm.

title:
Do US Public Pensions Manage Risk Effectively?

A Review of 38 Public Pensions
affiliations: Georgetown University - McDonough School of Business and Risktyle

detail.title:
Do US Public Pensions Manage Risk Effectively?

A Review of 38 Public Pensions
detail.abstract:
At the highest level, using historical data on performance, funded status, and asset allocations, the quantitative analysis suggests less than optimal management of the biggest risk, asset-liability risk, as the average funded status of public pensions in 2025 is approximately 80% (having been above 100% pre- 2000), with a very generous discount factor. In the next stage of managing assets, active management, there isn’t a high degree of confidence that these funds are skillful, and this is explained by the fact that effective control of volatility and drawdowns of the absolute and relative portfolios are less than ideal. Size does seem to be a negative factor in both funded status and skill, but these results are biased by the two largest public pension funds in California. However, the average results mask some exceptional funds and we examine qualitative aspects that lead to good outcomes.

The main takeaways are that in addition to selecting qualified staff, the public funds with the best funded status and risk management are those where there are: (i) effective governance and delegation of responsibilities between Boards and investment staff, (ii) continuity of tenure in both organizations, (iii) empowerment of staff to be long-term investors, and a (iv) collaborative environment. Ideally, public pension funds are not politicized as that conflicts with fiduciary duty. These conclusions offer useful lessons to countries seeking to establish or improve public management of assets.

title: Default Options and Market Power: Evidence from Target-Date Funds
affiliations: Bocconi University and London Business School

detail.title: Default Options and Market Power: Evidence from Target-Date Funds
detail.abstract: This paper studies how default investment options generate market power in the U.S. retirement savings market. Focusing on Target-Date Funds (TDFs), the predominant default option in 401(k) plans, we show that the incremental fees TDFs charge over their underlying funds increased from about 4 basis points in 2010 to over 17 basis points in 2022. This increase is consistent with rising market power among TDF managers, who exploit fee-insensitive default investors. To quantify this market power and evaluate policy interventions, we develop and estimate a structural model of demand and fee setting in both TDF and non-TDF markets. Preventing price discrimination between TDFs and non-TDFs increases TDF investors' welfare by $1.5 billion, with only modest reductions in fund manager profits.

title: Immigration and Inequality: A Micro-Macro Approach
affiliations: Norges Bank, Norges Bank and ETH Zurich

detail.title: Immigration and Inequality: A Micro-Macro Approach
detail.abstract: In this paper, we reconsider the link between immigration and labor income inequality using detailed micro and macro-data for Norway. The macro-data are needed to control for the fact that immigration responds to the state of the economy. The microdata are crucial to identify the heterogeneous effects of migration along the earnings distribution. We estimate a Factor Augmented Vector Autoregression (FAVAR) model tailored to include cross-sectional data to disentangle three immigration shocks (job-related, family reunifications and refugees). We find that immigration increases inequality not because workers at the bottom are more negatively affected but because workers at the top are benefiting disproportionately. This is clearly the case in response to job-related migration and to some extent also to family reunifications. Yet, results are clearly different in response to a refugee inflow. Thus, disentangling the reason for migration is of paramount importance.

title: How did Wells Fargo Adjust their Mortgage Activity in Response to their Asset Cap?
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System,  and Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.title: How did Wells Fargo Adjust their Mortgage Activity in Response to their Asset Cap?
detail.abstract: Using loan-level mortgage application data, we examine how Wells Fargo, a major originator in the U.S. mortgage market, adjusted its mortgage lending activity in response to a 2018 consent order that capped Wells Fargo's assets. We find that the bank received fewer loan applications and issued fewer loans relative to similar firms operating in the same county, with a cumulative reduction of growth by about 50 percentage points six years after the cap was imposed. We also present novel stylized facts on how Wells Fargo adjusted its balance sheet in response to the asset cap. We further find that relative to similar firms, Wells Fargo remained more active in refinancing loans than purchase loans, particularly during the 2021 refinance wave, during which the bank cut back more on jumbo mortgages than on conforming mortgages.

title: 1 Global sensitivity analysis workflows and rankings: a practical comparison for researchers
affiliations: University of Edinburgh, The James Hutton Institute, Norwegian Institute for Water Research, , The James Hutton Institute and Biomathematics and Statistics Scotland

detail.title: 1 Global sensitivity analysis workflows and rankings: a practical comparison for researchers
detail.abstract: Global sensitivity analysis (GSA) is a recommended step in the use of computer simulation models. GSA quantifies the relative importance of model inputs on outputs (Factor Ranking), identifies inputs that could be fixed, thus simplifying model calibration (Factor Fixing), and pinpointing areas for future data collection (Factor Prioritization). Given the wide variety of GSA methods, choosing between methods can be challenging for non-GSA experts. Issues include workflow steps and complexity, interpretation of GSA outputs, and the degree of similarity between methods in Factor Ranking. We conducted a study of both widely and less commonly used GSA methods applied to three simulators of differing complexity. All methods share common issues around implementation with specification of parameter ranges particularly critical. Similarities in Factor Rankings were generally high based on Kendall's W. Sobol' first order and total sensitivity indices were easy to interpret and informative with regression trees providing additional insight into interactions.

title: Quantifying Priorities in Business Cycle Reports: Analysis of Recurring Textual Patterns around Peaks and Troughs
affiliations: Helmut-Schmidt-University Hamburg

detail.title: Quantifying Priorities in Business Cycle Reports: Analysis of Recurring Textual Patterns around Peaks and Troughs
detail.abstract:
This paper proposes a novel method to uncover shifting priorities and links
them to macroeconomic fluctuations. To this end, I leverage quantitative
business cycle forecasts published by leading German economic research institutes
from 1970-2017 to estimate the proportions of latent topics. These
topics are then aggregated into broader macroeconomic subjects using a supervised
approach. By extracting the cyclical components of these subjects’
proportions, I derive dynamic measures of forecasters’ thematic priorities.
Correlating the cyclic components with key macroeconomic indicators reveals
consistent patterns across economic expansions and contractions. Around
economic peaks, forecasters emphasize inflation-related over recession-related
topics. I thus propose that forecasters’ failure to predict recessions may stem
from a tendency to underestimate growth risks and overestimate inflation
risks during periods of contractionary monetary policy. Around troughs,
forecasters prioritize investment-related topics over general growth considerations.

title: AI-Native Software Engineering and Vibe Coding: A Strategic Technical Survey for Modern Engineering Leadership(2025-2035)
affiliations: Fourth Industrial Systems Corporation

detail.title: AI-Native Software Engineering and Vibe Coding: A Strategic Technical Survey for Modern Engineering Leadership(2025-2035)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of Fourth Industrial Systems Corporation, an organization conducting research related to AI-native engineering, multi-agent systems, and governance technologies discussed in this paper. This affiliation may be perceived as relevant to the conceptual frameworks presented, but no financial or external influence shaped the analysis or conclusions.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants, medical or behavioral data, or interventions requiring IRB review. All materials synthesized derive from publicly accessible academic sources. Therefore, no ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The work was conducted independently by the author without financial support from government agencies, corporations, or academic institutions.

detail.abstract: This academic survey synthesizes the emerging discipline of AI-native software engineering, focusing on the evolution of vibe coding, agentic programming paradigms, and multiagent AI ecosystems. Drawing from over fifty contemporary research contributions, spanning cloud-agnostic infrastructures, multi-cloud orchestration, AI-native memory and compute systems, AI-native software engineering (SE 3.0), agentic DevSecOps, AI-native networking (6G), and trust-native governance, this paper characterizes the foundational architectures, workflows, and risks defining the next era of computational systems.

title: Causal Energy-Economic Growth Interactions Revisited: Decomposing Synergistic, Unique, and Redundant Components
affiliations: Forschungszentrum Jülich GmbH, Forschungszentrum Jülich GmbH, Forschungszentrum Jülich - Institute of Energy and Climate Research Systems Analysis and Technology Evaluation (IEK-STE) and Research Centre Jülich

detail.title: Causal Energy-Economic Growth Interactions Revisited: Decomposing Synergistic, Unique, and Redundant Components
detail.abstract: This paper examines the causal relationship between energy and economic growth (GDP). Utilizing the novel Synergistic-Unique-Redundant Decomposition method, it quantifies how much information about changes in energy and GDP is provided by their own past trends, by each other's influence, and by their combined effects. This advances the literature beyond traditional Granger causality methods, which cannot disentangle these components sufficiently. ........[..]

title: Idiosyncratic Risk Premium
affiliations: Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU) - Shanghai Advanced Institute of Finance (SAIF) and University of California, San Diego (UCSD) - Rady School of Management

detail.title: Idiosyncratic Risk Premium
detail.abstract: The market portfolio of U.S. stocks is highly concentrated, with market capitalization following a fat-tailed distribution. Under the Arbitrage Pricing Theory (Ross, 1976), the risk premium associated with idiosyncratic risk-the idiosyncratic risk premium (IRP)-is bounded-below and above-by the degree of market concentration, and non-zero if investors hold concentrated portfolios. We build a model to explicitly compute the IRP and show that it increases with both idiosyncratic volatility (IVol) and market capitalization. The latter dependence contrasts sharply with the negative relation between systematic risk premia and market capitalization in Fama-French factor models. For U.S. stocks, market capitalization is strongly negatively related to idiosyncratic volatility. In this case, the positive dependence of IRP on market cap implies an indirect negative relation with volatility. When this indirect effect outweighs the direct positive impact of volatility, IRP declines with IVol-resolving the IVol puzzle.

title: Visual Cues and Valuation: Evidence from the Housing Market
affiliations: University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, University of Arkansas, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville - Department of Finance,  and University of Connecticut - Department of Finance

detail.title: Visual Cues and Valuation: Evidence from the Housing Market

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Data provided by Zillow through the Zillow Transaction and Assessment Dataset (ZTRAX). More information on accessing the data can be found at http://www.zillow.com/ztrax. The results and opinions are those of the author(s) and do not reflect the position of Zillow Group. The survey experiment was pre-registered at the AEA RCT Registry titled “The Staging Effect during House Sales” (AEARCTR-0016398).
declarations.ethicsApproval: We obtained IRB approval (protocol# 2405543087) from the University of Arkansas.

detail.abstract: We examine the economic impact of non-consumable visual cues through home staging on high-stakes housing transactions. Using hand-collected listing photos for 15,777 transactions and a machine-learning algorithm to detect furniture, we provide the first large-scale evidence that staged homes sell for roughly 10% more and one week faster than comparable homes without furniture. Our pre-registered online experiment establishes causality and uncovers mechanisms.
